cases.name: ast: a plain navigation names itself by its last segment
cases.notes: `flatten` is a list of `flatten` nodes on the body, in writing order (`[]` when there is none — every body carries the field since 0.25). Without `as` a plain navigation binds its last segment, exactly as a select item or a group key is named, so `flatten tags` rebinds `tags` to each element.
cases.query: select name, tags from people flatten tags

cases.name: ast: `as` with the default name is the same tree
cases.notes: The tree does not record whether `as` was written: `name` is always filled, and the canonical printer always writes `as <name>` (AST.md §6), as it aliases every select item and every group key.
cases.query: select name, tags from people flatten tags as tags

cases.name: ast: a dotted navigation, `as`, and a chain reading an earlier name
cases.query: select name, t, kids from people flatten meta.tags as t flatten t.kids

cases.name: ast: the block is the implicit collect directive over the value
cases.notes: `flatten tags { … }` is `flatten tags collect { … }`: the brace after a receiver is the receiver-block sugar of GRAMMAR §2 (since 0.20 it stands wherever a value does), so the flattened value is a `collect` op and there is no block field of its own. A value that is not a plain navigation needs `as`.
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags { where $it != "b" } as t

cases.name: ast: a block with distinct, a projection, an order and a bound
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten jobs distinct { employer values order by pay desc limit 1 } as t

cases.name: ast: flatten inside a nested block
cases.notes: A block body carries `flatten` like the top level; the projection is evaluated after the fan-out, so `t: tags` reads the bound element.
cases.query: select name, jt: jobs collect { employer, t: tags flatten tags } from people

cases.name: ast spans: flatten with and without `as`
cases.notes: A `flatten` node spans the word through the name — or through the expression when `as` was omitted.
cases.query: select n from p flatten xs as x flatten ys

cases.name: an array fans out: one row per element, in collection order, the parent repeated; an empty array yields none
cases.query: select name, tags from people flatten tags

cases.name: the default name shadows the row's property; `as` keeps it readable
cases.query: select name, tags, t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: an object is one row, the object
cases.notes: SEMANTICS §3: a non-array object is one row; flatten binds it whole.
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: absent is one row with the name absent: a missing field never drops the row
cases.notes: Dataview's rule. Both spellings of absent (a missing key, `null`) are one value (§1).
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: a scalar is one row with the scalar: flatten splits a value, it does not source rows
cases.notes: The one deliberate softening of §3: a scalar in flatten position is not the `not a collection or an object` eval error, since no rows are sourced from it.
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: every kind at once, in parent order then element order
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: a template literal reads the bound name
cases.notes: An absent binding makes the literal absent (§7b).
cases.query: select label: `${name}:${t}` values from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: values over flattened rows
cases.query: select t values from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: the row's own properties, `$it` and `^` are unchanged on a flattened row
cases.notes: A flattened row IS the parent row with one more name bound at the same scope depth: `$it` is the row, `^` reads the enclosing scope.
cases.query: select name, me: $it.name, up: ^people.size(), t from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: a bound element may be navigated like any value
cases.query: select name, e: j.employer, p: j.pay from people flatten jobs as j

cases.name: a binding may be the flattened value

strings: select name, n from people flatten

cases.name: a block filters the elements first; a parent whose elements are all filtered away yields no row
cases.notes: The block is a `collect` over the value (§3): over Alice's `["b"]` it is `[]`, and over Carol's missing `tags` it is `[]` too (absent → no rows), so neither keeps a row — a block makes the value a collection. Without the block Carol would keep one row with `t` absent.
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags { where $it != "b" } as t

cases.name: a block may project, order and bound the elements
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten jobs { employer values order by pay desc limit 1 } as t

cases.name: a block that projects a record binds the record
cases.query: select name, e: j.e, p: j.pay from people flatten jobs { e: employer, pay where pay > 1 } as j

cases.name: distinct in the block dedups the elements
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags distinct { } as t

cases.name: a block over a single object is the record (§3), one row
cases.query: select name, h from people flatten home { city } as h

cases.name: a block over a single object that fails its where is absent: one row with the name absent
cases.notes: A `collect` over one object is the record or absent, never a list (§3); absent is one flattened row. Only a collection with no elements yields none.
cases.query: select name, h from people flatten home { where city == "LA" } as h

cases.name: a nested flatten inside the block fans the elements out before they are bound
cases.notes: The block is an ordinary select-position block, so every clause legal there is legal here. Its projection is what gets bound: with no projection the block yields its rows themselves, and a name bound inside it is not a property of those rows.
cases.query: select name, e: j.e, t: j.t from people flatten jobs { e: employer, t: tags flatten tags } as j

cases.name: a follow inside the block: the occurrences are the elements
cases.notes: The destination block's receiver is read in the frontier row's scope (depth 2), so the root is `^^tree` there; `^root` in the block's where reads Bob.
cases.query: select name, k: n.id from p flatten ^tree { where id == ^root follow ^^tree { where parent == ^id } } as n

cases.name: flattens chain: a cross product per row, parent order then element order
cases.query: select name, t, s from people flatten tags as t flatten sizes as s

cases.name: a later flatten reads an earlier bound name; an empty inner collection drops that element's rows
cases.query: select name, e: j.employer, jt from people flatten jobs as j flatten j.tags as jt

cases.name: a later flatten over an absent member of an earlier element keeps the row
cases.query: select name, e: j.employer, jt from people flatten jobs as j flatten j.tags as jt

cases.name: where filters rows before the fan-out, where the bound name is still the row's property
cases.notes: `where` runs per row before `flatten` (the clause order is the order of operations), so `t` there reads the row's own `t`; the projection reads the bound element.
cases.query: select name, t from people where t == "zz" flatten tags as t

cases.name: a from re-projection, then flatten
cases.query: people collect { e: employer, t from jobs flatten tags as t }

cases.name: a flatten fans a single receiver out: the block is plural
cases.notes: As a `from` re-projection and a `follow` do (§3).
cases.query: person collect { name, t flatten tags as t }

cases.name: $key of a flattened row is the pair (parent identity, element identity)
cases.notes: An entry's identity is its key (§21); the element's is its structural value. The pair is a two-element list, nested again by a later flatten (`[["x", 1], "a"]`) — never flattened, so `(p, [1, 2])` and a chained `(p, 1), 2` stay apart.
cases.query: select k: $key values from entries(m) flatten $it as t

cases.name: a chained flatten nests the pair
cases.query: select k: $key values from entries(m) flatten $it as t flatten t.tags as g

cases.name: an element that is an entry is known by its key
cases.notes: As a plain value an entry is a `{ key, value }` record (§21).
cases.query: select k: $key, e from entries(x) flatten entries($it) as e

cases.name: distinct over unprojected flattened rows dedups by the pair
cases.notes: Bob's two `a` elements are one identity `(Bob, "a")`; Al's `a` is another (a different parent).
cases.query: people count distinct { flatten tags as t }

cases.name: `is` compares the pair
cases.query: select hit: $key is ("x", 2) values from entries(m) flatten $it as t

cases.name: count counts the flattened rows
cases.notes: Bob two, Alice none (an empty list), Carol one (absent).
cases.query: people count { flatten tags as t }

cases.name: exists over flattened rows: a block that empties every parent is false
cases.query: people exists { flatten tags { where $it == "zz" } as t }

cases.name: first is the first flattened row
cases.notes: Alice's empty list yields nothing, so the first row comes from Bob.
cases.query: people first { name, t flatten tags as t }

cases.name: order by, limit and offset apply to the flattened rows
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t order by t limit 2 offset 1

cases.name: order by desc over the bound name, absent last
cases.query: select name, t from people flatten tags as t order by t desc

cases.name: group by a bound name: the flattened rows are grouped, absent with null
cases.query: select tags, n: count() from people flatten tags group by tags

cases.name: an aggregate reads the bound name on each flattened row; rows re-enters the rows themselves
cases.notes: `rows` is the group's rows (§24) — the host's rows, which carry no binding — so a bound name is read through an aggregate (`collect(t)`), on the row scopes the body kept.
cases.query: select t, who: collect(name), rs: rows collect { name } from people flatten tags as t group by t order by t

cases.name: the default projection of a grouped flattened body
cases.query: from people flatten tags as t group by t

cases.name: having over groups of flattened rows
cases.query: select t values from people flatten tags as t group by t having count() > 1

cases.name: count of flattened rows as a value, and in where
cases.query: select name, n: jobs count { flatten tags } from people where jobs count { flatten tags } > 2

cases.name: flatten after follow fans the occurrences out, in walk order then element order
cases.notes: The walk's intrinsics belong to the occurrence and are kept on every flattened row.
cases.query: select id, $depth, t from tree where id == 1 follow ^tree { where parent == ^id } flatten tags as t

cases.name: a where-position collect with lifts, then a flatten over the lifted list
cases.notes: A lift (§19) binds a list onto the row; `flatten` is its one-to-many sibling and may split it.
cases.query: select name, o from people where kids collect { ^o: name where ok } flatten o

cases.name: `flatten` and `as` are field names outside their position
cases.notes: A contextual word (GRAMMAR §1): `flatten` is a clause only when a value follows it.
cases.query: select flatten, as from r where flatten == 1 order by as

cases.name: `flatten` before a clause word is a field
cases.query: select flatten from r order by flatten

cases.name: error: flatten after group by
cases.query: from people group by city flatten tags

includes: OQX clause order is select, from, where, frontier, follow, flatten, group by, having, order by, limit, offset

cases.name: error: flatten after order by
cases.query: from people order by name flatten tags

includes: OQX clause order is select, from, where, frontier, follow, flatten, group by, having, order by, limit, offset

cases.name: error: follow after flatten
cases.query: from people flatten tags follow kids

includes: OQX clause order is select, from, where, frontier, follow, flatten, group by, having, order by, limit, offset

cases.name: error: where after flatten
cases.query: from people flatten tags where name == "Bob"

includes: OQX clause order is select, from, where, frontier, follow, flatten, group by, having, order by, limit, offset

cases.name: error: flatten after group by inside a destination block
cases.notes: Inside a destination block the order sentence names `depth` too.
cases.query: from t follow kids { group by k flatten tags }

includes: frontier, depth, follow, flatten, group by

cases.name: error: an expression needs a name
cases.notes: Only a plain navigation names itself.
cases.query: from people flatten size(tags)

cases.name: error: a block needs a name
cases.query: from people flatten tags { where $it != "b" }

cases.name: error: a tuple needs a name
cases.query: from people flatten (tags, aliases)

cases.name: error: duplicate flatten name
cases.query: from people flatten tags as t flatten kids as t

cases.name: error: duplicate flatten name by default
cases.query: from people flatten tags flatten tags

cases.name: error: a reserved word after as
cases.query: from people flatten tags as from

cases.name: error: a literal word after as
cases.query: from people flatten tags as null

cases.name: error: a $-name after as
cases.notes: `$` belongs to the language (SEMANTICS §2).
cases.query: from people flatten tags as $it

cases.name: error: nothing after as
cases.query: from people flatten tags as

cases.name: error: flatten with nothing after it
cases.notes: Without a value after it `flatten` is a stray field name; the message says what the clause needs.
cases.query: from people flatten

cases.name: error: an aggregate in a flatten expression
cases.notes: The rows are not grouped yet when `flatten` runs.
cases.query: from people flatten collect(tags) as t group by city

includes: `collect(tags)` is an aggregate and cannot be read in `flatten`

cases.name: error: a lift inside a flatten block
cases.notes: The block is a select-position block, not a where-position `collect`.
cases.query: from people flatten jobs { ^x: pay } as j

cases.name: error: a bound name is not a group key
cases.notes: After `group by` the body reads the group (§24); a flattened row's binding is read through a key or an aggregate.
cases.query: select t from people flatten tags as t group by city

includes: `t` is not a group key or aggregate

cases.name: references: the flatten expression is read on the rows; the bound name is not a reference after it
cases.notes: `t` in the select and in `order by` is the name the flatten bound — an alias of the expression already reported, like a lift — so neither is a reference; the scope's row chain is unchanged (a flattened row is the row).
cases.query: select name, t from people where active flatten tags as t order by t

cases.name: references: names inside the block are read on the elements, one deeper
cases.notes: The block is the `collect` op over the value: its receiver is a step like any block receiver, so a host judges `typ` against the kind `blocks` yields.
cases.query: select name from people flatten blocks { where typ == "task" } as b

cases.name: references: a chain reading an earlier name, and a name's own expression
cases.notes: `j.tags` is headed by the bound `j` and `j.kind` in the select likewise: not references. The third flatten's `tags` reads the row (its own name is bound only after it), so it is a reference.
cases.query: select name, k: j.kind from people flatten jobs as j flatten j.tags as t flatten tags

cases.name: references: ^name from a nested block reads the bound name
cases.query: select name, m: kids collect { where x == ^t } from people flatten tags as t

cases.name: references: a bound name as a group key is not a reference; before the flatten it is the row's
cases.notes: `where` runs before the fan-out, so `t` there is the row's property (no select item names `t`, else §14's alias rule would already exclude it); the key `t` reads the binding.
cases.query: select n: count() from people where t == 1 flatten tags as t group by t
